title: Our sim bots said wave 15 was a difficulty wall. It was the bot. Building a 200-enemy phone roguelite with AI, and what still needed a human (DeepForge, closed test open)
author: DigiCoreStudios
selftext:
We're a tiny studio making AnvilHeart: DeepForge, a survivor-style roguelite for Android. You pick a dwarf hero, delve chapter by chapter, and hold off a few hundred cave creatures at once. Between runs you forge and fuse gear. The closed test just opened, so here's how it's been built, including the parts where the AI got it wrong.



\*\*Who does what\*\*

One human directs: design calls, game feel, what ships. Every line of game code is written by Claude Code, with separate sessions for the game, the art and the audio, and one more that checks each release before it goes out.



\*\*3D models: image-to-3D, but hand-made animation\*\*

Heroes and enemies are image-to-3D meshes (Tripo). The animation is not AI: every clip, from idle and run to every enemy gait (hop, crawl, stomp, glide, scuttle), is hand-keyed through Blender Python scripts. We tried AI animation and it wasn't good enough for us.



\*\*The swarm: vertex animation textures\*\*

Hundreds of skinned meshes would melt a phone, so each enemy's animation is baked into textures, and one MultiMesh draw call per enemy type animates the whole swarm in the shader. Our phone gate was 200 enemies on screen, and it ran at 120 fps on our test phone (p99 frame time 9.1 ms) before the camera change below. Generated meshes have hard face budgets for that: 2,500 for swarm enemies, 6,000 for elites, 20,000 for heroes and bosses.



\*\*1. The bugs the tests couldn't see\*\*

For a while the baker grabbed the rest pose for every frame, so no enemy actually animated in game, and every automated test still passed. Someone finally looked at the screen.



Later, a tester reached wave 17 of the endless mode and every enemy and projectile vanished, while the hero and floor stayed. The swarm's draw batches had a fixed culling box of ±1000 m around the map origin. Kite in one direction for long enough and you walk out of it, so the GPU culls the entire swarm. Our sim bots run in circles near the origin and never got that far. The fix was one number (the box is now a million metres), plus a new test that starts a run 1,500 m out. The AI writes good tests for everything you describe. It couldn't think of "a player who just keeps running east".



\*\*2. Measuring a rival's camera from one screenshot\*\*

A tester couldn't spot enemy shots, so we gave the AI a screenshot of a popular game in the genre and asked it to measure. Hero width as a share of screen width: 6.4% there, 11.1% in ours. We were about 1.7× too zoomed in, showing roughly a third of the ground. We pulled the camera back 1.7×, and then enemy shots looked tiny, so they're now drawn 1.5× bigger with the same hitboxes. Draw calls went from 54 to 69, and it still holds 60 fps with 200 enemies on our desktop benchmark. Turning "hard to see" into a number made the fix a single camera setting instead of guesswork.



\*\*3. When the bot is the bug\*\*

We balance with headless sim bots: a "camper" that stands still and an active player. After we added per-zone hazards (lava, floodwater, spore clouds), every bot died at exactly wave 15. It looked like a difficulty wall. It was the bot: its "avoid the slowing water" steering pushed it straight into the boss. Once we taught it to dodge only damaging pools, the wall disappeared.



Then our human tester hit a real wall at wave 24. So enemy HP growth went from 12% to 9% per wave, the every-10-waves HP jump from ×1.25 to ×1.15, and giants moved from wave 20 to 25. Active bots now die around waves 27 to 29, while campers still die by wave 10 to 16. Bots find regressions fast, but only a person can tell you when it feels unfair.



\*\*Audio\*\*

Nearly all music and SFX come from Stable Audio Open. We generate six takes per sound and keep the best two to five as variants. The newer per-zone shot-warning sounds were also ranked by an audio-text model (CLAP) and filtered for a sharp start (peak within 0.1 s) so they read as warnings. The real work is the finishing: trimming silence, cutting tails, evening out loudness and making loops seamless. Every third-party and model licence ships in the app on a Credits & licences screen.



\*\*Smaller ones\*\*

\- Some projectile art went through image-to-3D, and the first pass turned 3 of 5 into flat dishes and boxes, because glow and sparks in the source images confused the 3D step. Redrawn as solid shapes first, they came out right.

\- Builds 20 to 29 went from code to the Play closed test in about 4 days, with a scripted export and upload to Play's internal test and one manual click to promote each build to the closed test.

\- The clips we post are rendered by a scripted recorder in the game, not screen-captured.



\*\*Want to try it?\*\*

The closed test is open on Android, and it's free to play. Sign up with the Google account you use on the Play Store and you'll get the tester link right away (the Play listing can take a few minutes to appear): [https://digicore.studio/deepforge-alpha](https://digicore.studio/deepforge-alpha)



We'd love to hear where you died and whether it felt fair, and anything that stuttered on your phone (please tell us the model).



Happy to go deeper on any of it: VAT baking, sim-bot balancing, measuring "game feel", or what still needs a human in the loop.
